originalTitle: 卖内存的万亿狂欢，买内存的利润腰斩
title: Memory Sellers' Trillion-Dollar Frenzy, Memory Buyers' Profit Halved
oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the structural divergence in the memory chip industry: AI memory demand has propelled Micron's market cap past one trillion, while smartphone maker Xiaomi's profits have been halved due to soaring memory costs. It also questions whether Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) can truly eliminate the cyclical nature of the memory industry.
summary: Using the contrasting events of Xiaomi's profit plunge and Micron's market cap hitting one trillion on May 26, 2026, as a starting point, this article delves into the intense divergence currently unfolding in the memory chip industry. The core argument is that AI-driven memory demand (HBM, server DDR5) and consumer-grade memory (smartphones, PCs) have formed a three-tiered, diverging market. The article focuses on the new narrative of Long-Term Agreements (LTAs), arguing that 3-5 year fixed-price contracts signed by cloud providers to secure AI memory capacity could fundamentally alter the cyclical nature of the memory industry, shifting memory stocks from cyclical valuations to infrastructure utility valuations. However, the author remains cautious, pointing out that the premise for LTAs to eliminate cyclicality is that AI demand does not collapse. It warns that Micron's current high valuation is based on peak-cycle earnings, posing a risk of a Davis Double Play. The article also highlights the significant market disagreement over a memory super-cycle, using the example of Goldman Sachs missing out on Micron's rally.

mainPoints.point: AI memory demand and consumer-grade memory markets are severely diverging.
mainPoints.explanation: HBM and server DDR5 are seeing price hikes and shortages due to the AI arms race, while mobile memory prices are also rising but squeezing profits. In contrast, the PC retail market is even experiencing price cuts to clear inventory, forming a three-tiered divergence.

mainPoints.point: Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) are seen as a new narrative to eliminate memory cyclicality.
mainPoints.explanation: Cloud providers are signing 3-5 year fixed-price contracts with memory manufacturers to lock in AI memory capacity. This could shift the valuation of memory stocks from cyclical (8-15x P/E) to utility-like (20-30x P/E), which is the core logic behind Micron's stock surge.

mainPoints.point: The premise for LTAs to eliminate cyclicality is sustained high growth in AI demand; otherwise, there is a risk of a Davis Double Play.
mainPoints.explanation: Micron's current trillion-dollar market cap is built on peak-cycle earnings. If AI capital expenditure growth slows, growth driven by price elasticity rather than volume elasticity will be very fragile, potentially repeating Cisco's valuation collapse after the internet bubble.

mainPoints.point: Goldman Sachs' conservative stance on Micron reflects significant disagreement in the market regarding a super-cycle.
mainPoints.explanation: While Wall Street was largely bullish on Micron, Goldman Sachs maintained a neutral rating and missed the rally. Its cautious stance warrants consideration, highlighting potential risks in the market consensus.

keyQuotes: On the same day, memory sellers reveled in a trillion-dollar frenzy, while memory buyers saw their profits halved.
Valuing a company by multiplying peak-cycle earnings by a seemingly 'reasonable' multiple to arrive at a seemingly 'not expensive' valuation is the classic valuation trap when cyclical stocks peak.
The very moment long-term agreements are truly needed is precisely when they are most likely to fail.
When the entire Wall Street chorus sings 'this time is different,' it's at least worth pausing to ask: what happened the last time everyone was so certain?
